question: A Deployment named search-ranking runs 20 replicas with a rolling update strategy of maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, chosen to guarantee zero downtime. An engineer runs kubectl set image. The new ReplicaSet's pod starts, but one pod immediately fails its livenessProbe and enters CrashLoopBackOff, never becoming Ready; the other new pods are healthy and Ready. Explain precisely why this rollout becomes stuck partway and will not progress to completion, describe what the Deployment controller does with both ReplicaSets during the stall, and give the exact set of commands to confirm the stuck state and recover cleanly without violating the zero-downtime policy?
answer: With maxUnavailable: 0, the controller may not terminate any old pod, so it can only add new pods up to the surge capacity of maxSurge: 1. That single surge slot is consumed by a CrashLooping pod that never becomes Ready, and since zero old pods can be scaled down, the rollout stalls. kubectl rollout status search-ranking blocks waiting for completion. kubectl rollout undo search-ranking reverts the template to the previous ReplicaSet and terminates the bad pods.
explanation:
## How It Works

The Deployment controller drives a rolling update toward the desired state while honoring two independent constraints. maxSurge caps how many extra pods may exceed the desired replica count, and maxUnavailable caps how many pods may be down below it. Setting maxUnavailable: 0 forces the controller to keep every old pod healthy at all times, so the only headroom for scaling is the surge surplus allowed by maxSurge.

With maxSurge: 1 and 20 replicas desired, the controller creates the surge pod on top of the 20 running old pods, for 21 total. Before it can terminate any old pod, the surge pod must become Ready, because no old pod may be deleted while maxUnavailable is 0. A pod that fails its livenessProbe never reaches Ready "True". That single surge slot stays occupied by the unusable CrashLooping pod, so the controller is permitted to create exactly zero further new pods and zero deletions. The rollout is therefore deadlocked at roughly "1 new, 19 old," with the new ReplicaSet unable to grow and the old one unable to shrink.

The stall is visible because the Deployment's observedGeneration field is behind its metadata.generation, and kubectl rollout status blocks with a "Waiting for deployment ... rollout to finish" message. This is a physical headroom problem, not a pod scheduling one, so it will not self-heal or time out; it requires a template change or an explicit rollback to break the stall.

## Code Example

```bash
# Confirm the stuck rollout and replicate counts
kubectl rollout status deployment/search-ranking
# Waiting for deployment "search-ranking" rollout to finish: 0 out of 1 new replicas have been updated...

kubectl get rs -l app=search-ranking
# NAME                    DESIRED  CURRENT  READY  AGE
# search-ranking-5f7d   1        1        0      3m   <- new, CrashLooping surge
# search-ranking-2k9p   19       19       19     6d   <- old RS, cannot be scaled down

kubectl get pods -l app=search-ranking
# ... observe the new pod in CrashLoopBackOff with a liveness probe failure

# Inspect rollout status and the reason it is blocked
kubectl describe deployment/search-ranking

# Recover: roll back the template to the previous ReplicaSet
kubectl rollout undo deployment/search-ranking

# Alternative recovery after fixing the image if the bug is understood
kubectl set image deployment/search-ranking search-ranking=search-ranking:v4
```

With maxUnavailable: 0, a rollback works because reverting the template to the old revision makes the old ReplicaSet the desired one again; the controller sacrifices the single bad surge pod (by scaling its ReplicaSet to zero) and leave the healthy old pods untouched, preserving zero downtime.

## Key Points

- **maxSurge** grants the only scale-out headroom when maxUnavailable is 0
- **A CrashLooping surge pod** can consume that single slot forever, keeping the rollout from progressing
- **Rollout stall** is signaled by stuck kubectl rollout status and by observedGeneration lagging metadata.generation
- **kubectl rollout undo** breaks the deadlock by flipping the template back to the prior revision

## Common Mistake

The most common error is assuming a rolling update will "just keep trying" or eventually catch up on its own. With maxUnavailable: 0, a single permanently-failing surge pod is a hard stop, because the controller is structurally forbidden from deleting any old pod to make room. Developers often respond by deleting the healthy old pods manually to force the new ReplicaSet up, which actually removes the pods that were protecting zero-downtime; deleting a CrashLooping pod is also futile because its ReplicaSet recreates it. The correct recovery is to change the pod template (fixed image or kubectl rollout undo) so the controller re-evaluates which ReplicaSet satisfies the desired state.

## Interview Tip

The interviewer is listening for a precise mental model of how maxUnavailable and maxSurge interact as constraints on the same rollout, not just the recipe. A strong answer states that maxUnavailable: 0 removes the option to shrink the old ReplicaSet, so progression depends entirely on the single surge slot becoming Ready. A great answer goes further and explains why the failure does not time out or self-heal, and why rollout undo (a template change) is the correct lever rather than deleting pods by hand. Mention that the surge slot count (maxSurge: 1) is exactly the width of the stall.
